zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-check: supplied [Entry Words Data of Nippojisho](https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html), NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Consulted after independent scan reading; the transcription corrections and English notes are this reviewer's work, not a reproduction of the lexical dataset.

runs.text: O dar, ou mandar carta. Vt,

lines.note: Keitat denotes giving or sending a letter. Va- starts vazato, the adverb introducing the respectful epistolary example on the next row.
The writer states that the letter is sent expressly for the purpose. The historical formula xexime ſoro is retained; depro- continues in the Portuguese translation.
Completes deproposito esta carta, sending this letter deliberately or expressly. The printed joined form is not modernized to a separate phrase.

Keitei means brothers, explained by ani and ototo. The printed vototo has no supplied length mark; the Portuguese explicitly specifies male siblings. The separate S. usage label is printed upright. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Keitō means leaning or toppling, explained by taore katamuku. The headword carries a caron, unlike the following flower-related circumflex forms.

Completes the gloss as being about to fall. The historical pera and the final written-register label are retained. The separate S. usage label is printed upright. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Keitō is explained literally as a chicken's head and referred to keitōge. The printed circumflex and the alternative marker l. are preserved.
The entry identifies a flower or herb and directs the reader to Qeitôgue. The Japanese cross-reference remains roman, separate from the italic Portuguese instruction.

runs.text: Roſa, ou flor de hũa certa erua q̃

lines.note: Keitōge denotes the flower of an herb, whose distinguishing appearance follows below. The circumflex and the Portuguese abbreviation q̃ remain as printed.

runs.text: ſe parece como crista de galo. ¶ Item, A

lines.note: The flower resembles a cock's comb, explaining the preceding chicken-head gloss. A second sense begins with the article A and names the plant itself.
Completes the second sense as the same herb, in addition to its flower. This short row closes the botanical entry.

Keion denotes a great benefaction, explained by megumi and on. The broad mark in võ is read as an abbreviation tilde, not the OCR's caron; the impression is thick, so the distinction is noted. The separate S. usage label is printed upright. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.

Keisha means a light carriage, explained by karuki kuruma. The written-register label accompanies the concise vehicle definition. The separate S. usage label is printed upright. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Keisei denotes a courtesan or prostitute in this gloss. Keisei wo tatsuru begins the example of practising that occupation and continues after ta-.
Completes the example and explains it as carrying on the occupation of a public woman. The historical wording is retained without euphemistic substitution in the transcription.

runs.text: O abater, ou deſprezar a alguem.

lines.note: Keisen means lowering or treating someone with contempt. The next example specifies the contemptuous manner of treatment.
Hito wo keisen ni atsukau means treating someone with contempt. The printed historical atçucǒ is retained, and al- continues in alguem below.
Completes the translation as treating someone basely or contemptuously. The short line closes the example, not a separate entry.
Keiset combines firefly and snow, as the Japanese hotaru and yuki make explicit. The following example applies the paired images to diligent study.
Completes the literal snow gloss and introduces accumulating the merit of firefly-and-snow study. The circumflex in côuo is preserved, and Eſ- starts estudar below.

runs.text: tudar, ou por diligencia no estudo de dia, &

lines.note: The Portuguese interprets the expression as studying diligently by day and night. The coordinated night phrase is printed on the next row.

runs.text: de noite: tomouſe a metafora de hũ eſtudante q̃

lines.note: Completes day-and-night study and introduces the dictionary's explanation of the metaphor through a student. Both printed abbreviation tildes are retained.

runs.text: na China à claridade daquelle bichinho, & da

lines.note: The student in China is said to have studied by the insect's light and by snow. This continues the source's own account without adding unprinted names.

runs.text: neue estudaua por não ter candea.

lines.note: Completes the story: the student used that light because he had no lamp. The historical candea spelling remains unchanged.
This keishi means hens' eggs. It is a separate homograph from the plant and temple-visiting entries that follow.

runs.text: Ramos de hũa certa aruore. ¶ Item,

lines.note: Another keishi denotes branches of a particular tree. A second botanical sense begins with Item and is explained on the next row.

runs.text: Hũa laya de canela que ſerue de mezinha.

lines.note: The additional sense is a kind of cinnamon used medicinally, as stated by the historical dictionary. The transcription does not add a modern species or treatment claim.

runs.text: Ir à varela, ou aos Camis,

lines.note: The verb describes going to a temple or to kami and buddhas. Camis is the Japanese religious term adapted within the Portuguese sentence; the coordination continues below.

Fotoques completes the reference to buddhas or their images in the temple-visiting definition. It is a Japanese-derived term within Portuguese prose, followed by the written-register label. The separate S. usage label is printed upright. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Keishin is glossed as wild cinnamon. The brief historical identification is retained without supplying a botanical species absent from the page.
Keishō denotes courtly rank associated with the kuge. The initial Q replaces OCR D; Cungues is embedded in Portuguese, while the repeated Qeixǒ begins an example.

runs.text: Cungues, ou fidalgos nobres que ſer-

lines.note: Unkaku completes keishō unkaku, explained as kuge or noble courtiers. The Portuguese ſer- begins servem, continued on the next row.
Completes ſer-uem and identifies service in the Dairi's household. Dairi is the Japanese court designation embedded in the Portuguese explanation.

Keishū is explained by karuki fune, a light vessel. The final caron distinguishes this nautical headword from the unaccented reverence entry immediately below. The separate S. usage label is printed upright. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.

runs.text: Certa reuerencia que ſe faz na China.

lines.note: Keishu is a particular act of reverence performed in China. The headword's final u has no caron here, unlike the preceding light-vessel entry.

The written-register label completes the preceding definition; a paragraph mark introduces keishu saifai. Its Portuguese explanation begins with performing adoration or reverence. The opening S. is upright, separate from the italic Portuguese apparatus. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Completes the example's definition as making reverence twice. This is a continuation of Qeixu ſaifai rather than a new entry.
Keiyaku means a promise or agreement. The paragraph example starts with Qei- and continues as yacu on the next physical row; the printed hyphen is retained.
Completes Qei-yacu and gives suru or mōsu as alternative verbs. The Portuguese gloss begins promising or making an agreement and continues below.
Completes fazer concerto, to make an agreement, in the preceding example. The short continuation row is not a separate headword.
Keiei is explained by the Japanese expression printed as Fe itonamu and by preparing or arranging a feast. The Portuguese con- continues into certar below.
Completes the feast-preparation definition and supplies keiei suru as its example. The Japanese example is roman within the surrounding italic Portuguese.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Negocear, ou grangear a vida, &

lines.note: Introduces an additional sense of conducting business or earning a living. The paragraph mark and Item belong to the Portuguese explanation rather than to a new entry.
Completes the additional business or livelihood sense by extending it to other things. This short line continues the same Qeiyei entry.
Keieki is explained by karuku and yasushi, light and easy. The Portuguese gloss confirms both qualities, with the second on the next row.
Completes the description as easy. It remains an indented continuation of Qeiyeqi, not a standalone entry.
Keiyō is explained by katachi and kao, form and face. The final ô and the historical spellings catachi and cauo are retained.
Keizu is explained as a written record of a household's standing. The Portuguese begins defining a book of genealogy or family lineage and continues on the next row.

runs.text: da gèração, ou de linhagẽ dalgũa familia.

lines.note: Completes the genealogical definition of Qeizzu. The grave accent in gèração and the abbreviation tildes in linhagẽ and dalgũa are retained from the print.
Kemange is identified only as a flower with this name. No botanical identification is supplied beyond the dictionary's brief Portuguese gloss.
Kemawashi is the verb of moving the hakama deftly with the feet. The embedded Japanese garment name is divided Faca-mas across physical rows, with the printed hyphen retained.

runs.text: mas que arrojão andando no Zaxiqui destramẽ-

lines.note: Completes Facamas and describes the trailing garment in a zashiki. The small raised terminal mark after destramẽ is a continuation hyphen, not the OCR's full stop; te follows below.

runs.text: te com os pees. ¶ Item, Fazer andar à

lines.note: Completes destramẽ-te and the first sense of using the feet deftly. A new sense begins with making something go around with the feet.

runs.text: roda com os pès algũa couſa como bola, &c.

lines.note: Completes the second sense with an object such as a ball. The partly worn nasal vowel in algũa is u rather than OCR a; the printed grave accent in pès is retained.
The noun kemawashi denotes the lower portions of long trousers. The description continues below and is separate from the preceding verb entry.

runs.text: ſe custumão nos Zaxiquis ſolemnes, ou de

lines.note: The long trousers are customary at formal zashiki gatherings or banquets. The damaged st ligature supports custumão, restoring the t lost in OCR cusumão; the baseline short s is retained rather than reclassified from the ligature's tall stroke. Zaxiquis is embedded in Portuguese prose.
Completes the reference to banquet occasions in the kemawashi definition. It is an indented continuation, with no new Japanese headword.
Kemi is explained by miru koto, seeing. Both the Japanese synonym and the brief Portuguese gloss support this reading without additional supplied text.

runs.text: O andar ordinario do caualo ſem cor-

lines.note: Kemichi denotes a horse's ordinary walking gait, contrasted with faster gaits. The final cor- is continued as rer on the next physical row.
Completes the contrast with running or trotting, then begins an example about a horse with a good gait. The line-end letter is v, not OCR y, and v-ma continues uma below.
Completes the divided v-ma and glosses kemichi no yoi uma as a horse with a good gait. The Japanese continuation remains roman and the Portuguese italic.
Kemyō is explained by kari no na, an ordinary or provisional name. The final long-vowel mark in Qemiǒ is visibly a caron and is retained.

runs.text: que ſe hum chama vniuerſalmente. Vide,

lines.note: Completes the description of the name by which someone is commonly called. Vide introduces the separate cross-reference printed on the next row.
The cross-reference Iitmiǒ, jitsumyō, contrasts with the ordinary or provisional name in Qemiǒ. Its final caron and the historical medial t are retained.

Kemō is explained by koi negai nozomu, longing or wishing, and by Portuguese desejo. The entry ends with the written-register label rather than an example. The separate S. usage label is printed upright. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Kemuri is the verb meaning to smoke or for smoke to rise. The large initial has the tail of Q, replacing OCR C; the Portuguese aleuan- continues below.
Completes aleuan-tarſe fumo, smoke rising. This belongs to the verb entry, before the distinct noun Qemuri on the following row.
Kemuri is the noun smoke. The paragraph example kemuri o tatsuru describes raising smoke; tatçuru retains the dictionary's cedilla spelling.
Glosses the preceding transitive example, then introduces kemuri ga agaru, smoke rising. The two Japanese examples are separated by the printed paragraph mark.
Tatçu is an alternative to agaru in the rising-smoke example. A further example begins with Qe-, continued by murini on the next physical row.
Completes Qe-murini me ga kururu, being unable to see because of smoke. The Portuguese confirms obstruction of vision rather than a new sense of the headword.
Restores the clearly printed paragraph mark omitted by OCR before the smoke-saturated example. The Portuguese mui- continues into to, describing being heavily smoked or smoke-stained.
Completes muito defumado, then introduces kemuri ni musebu, choking on smoke. The historical x spelling in muxebu is retained rather than modernized.
Glosses choking with smoke, then explicitly introduces a metaphorical use. Vo- begins the Japanese omoi expression and is continued on the next row.

Completes Vo-moino qemuri muneni mitçu, the smoke of thoughts filling the breast. The source marks this written usage and starts the Portuguese Eſ-tar gloss across rows. The intervening S. label is upright before the italic Portuguese gloss. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Completes the figurative explanation as being full of cares. The historical cheo spelling and the physical continuation from Eſ- are preserved.
Kemuridashi is glossed as a chimney. The final vowel of Chaminè carries the short grave-like accent visible in the scan.

runs.text: Couſa que faz fumo aos olhos, ou

lines.note: Kemutai describes something smoky to the eyes or the sensation of smoke in them. The definition continues below, followed by two related forms on their own rows.
Completes the alternative description of feeling smoke in the eyes. It remains part of the Qemutai entry rather than an independent phrase.
Kemutasa is the nominal form associated with the preceding smoky-to-the-eyes adjective. The isolated form is visibly indented under that entry and has no separate Portuguese gloss.
Kemutō is another form grouped under Qemutai. Its final caron and indented, otherwise unglossed presentation are preserved.
Kemushi is a hairy caterpillar or worm, literally glossed as a creature with hairs. The headword begins a new entry at the main text margin.
Ken is explained by kashikoi and prudence or wisdom. The example begins kennaru; the visible final u, omitted by OCR, is restored before fito on the next row.

runs.text: O homẽ prudẽte he raro. S.

lines.note: Completes kennaru hito mare nari, a wise person is rare. The first letter of homẽ is the b-like italic h also seen in he on this row; OCR b is corrected, and both abbreviation tildes are retained. The separate S. usage label is printed upright. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
This distinct ken, with the alternative kenpei, means authority or power. It is separate from the preceding prudence entry despite the identical headword spelling.
Ken o katte mono o yū introduces speaking by borrowed authority. The Portuguese begins the explanation of saying or commanding on behalf of someone with power.

runs.text: mãdar algũa couſa da parte de quem pode, ou

lines.note: Continues the explanation as ordering something in the name of someone able to command. The tilde abbreviations mãdar and algũa are preserved rather than expanded.
Completes the explanation of speaking or commanding on another's authority. The short row continues the preceding example without introducing a headword.

Ken-i o furū means displaying authority and magnificence. OCR Qenai is corrected to Qen-i: the scan shows a small raised separator before a distinct dotted i, not an a; the short separator is rendered as a hyphen.
Ken o or kenpei o ubō introduces taking another person's authority. The full stop after Qenuo, the alternative marker l, and the final caron in vbǒ follow the print.

runs.text: ſenhorio, ou poder dalguem por força.

lines.note: Completes the definition as taking someone's lordship or power by force. This remains the explanation of the preceding authority-taking example.
A new ken means humility, explained by herikudari. Its example begins Qen- and continues beyond this page; the lower-right ni co- is separate catchword furniture, not another body row.
Lower-right catchword following the body-line Qen-. The printed ni co- is retained as furniture and is not duplicated into the running text; the next page is not supplied.
